title: Geohash Encoder: Coordinates as Short Strings
description: Encode coordinates as geohash strings with the Geohash Encoder — cell size by length, database-friendly proximity keys. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Times Square encodes as dr5ru7 at six characters — and every point starting dr5ru shares its ~1.2 × 0.6 km cell, which is exactly how databases fake 'nearby' with a string prefix.
quick_answer: The Geohash Encoder encodes coordinates as geohash strings — short base-32 codes that identify map cells, with cell size set by the string's length. Enter the point and read its geohash — the key format databases use for proximity lookups and shareable place references.

body.t: Store the hash beside the point; prefix queries fetch the neighbourhood. The encoder lets you mint and inspect keys while designing — the
A stored hash decodes to its cell here in spirit — mismatched hashes beside known coordinates expose swapped axes in legacy data.
A 4–5 character hash shares a neighbourhood without sharing an address — precision as a dial, turned by string length.
Cell strings name cached areas tidily. The encoder shows which cell a point's cached data lives under.
57.64911, 10.40744 encodes to u4pruydqqvj — the worked example from the geohash literature, reproduced here as a correctness receipt for the algorithm.

Times Square dr5ru7 and a point across the park in the same cell share the prefix; two points metres apart across a cell border share almost nothing. Prefix search must fetch neighbouring cells too — the classic geohash caveat, stated on its own page.

popular_table.intro: Geohash cell dimensions (approximate, at the equator) — length is the precision dial.
popular_table.note: Cells are rectangles in degrees, so their ground size shrinks in width toward the poles. The base-32 alphabet omits a, i, l, o to dodge look-alike characters.

faq: What cell size do I get?
Chosen by string length — the table on this page maps characters to cell dimensions. Longer is smaller, by a factor of 32 per character (8×4 per step in ground terms, roughly).
Is it the same as a Plus Code?
No — different systems (Google's Open Location Code versus the public-domain geohash). Both turn coordinates into strings; their alphabets, cells and ecosystems differ.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 coordinates — geohashes encode the pair as given.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
The hash analogue: more characters mean smaller cells, not truer points. A 12-character hash of a bad fix is a precise lie.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Hashes paste as text attributes; most GIS and databases (PostGIS, MongoDB, Redis) speak geohash natively or by extension.
The border problem?
Neighbouring points across a cell edge share no prefix. Production proximity search queries the 8 surrounding cells as well — the encoder's cell view makes the fix intuitive.
Decode a hash?
The cell a hash names can be read back to its bounds — encoders in this family show the cell for any hash you bring.
Who invented it?
Gustavo Niemeyer, 2008, released into the public domain — one of the internet's quiet load-bearing ideas.
Case sensitivity?
Geohashes are lowercase by convention (the alphabet excludes ambiguous letters); systems store them lowercase.
Privacy of short hashes?
A 4-character hash is a region-sized fuzz — the string-length dial is a legitimate privacy control, sized by the table.
Sorting property?
Lexicographic order approximates spatial order (a Z-order curve) — good enough for prefix scans, which is the entire trick.
